title: Explanation of Benefits and Remittance Advice

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish an Explanation of Benefits from a remittance advice, including who receives each and how each is used.
- Interpret payment, adjustment, and patient responsibility amounts on an EOB and a remittance advice, including group and reason codes.
- Post payments and adjustments accurately to the correct patient account and claim line, and reconcile posted totals to funds received.
- Recognize when to escalate discrepancies, overpayments, credit balances, refunds, and cost-sharing questions to billing or authorized staff per office policy.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

An EOB is like the receipt and note a store mails you after a purchase to show what your membership card covered and what is left for you to pay.

### Question 2

An EOB is like a note explaining a bill that will come later, not the bill itself.

### Question 3

A remittance advice is like the packing slip and receipt a store sends with your refund to show exactly what was credited and why.

### Question 4

The 835 is like a standardized digital receipt format every store agrees to use so computers everywhere can read it the same way.

### Question 5

An EOB is like a receipt that still prints even when a coupon covers the whole price, so you can see what happened.

### Question 6

It is like one receipt described two ways: a plain-English note for the customer and a detailed ledger entry for the store.

### Question 7

An EOB is like a scorecard for one claim that shows who paid what and why.

### Question 8

A remittance advice is like a detailed deposit slip showing each payment and why the amount is what it is.

### Question 9

It is like having a bookkeeper receive the bank statement so they can record each deposit for the business.

### Question 10

The subscriber is like the named person on a family membership card whose benefits everyone else on the plan uses.

### Question 11

The allowed amount is like the agreed price a store and a discount card company set before the sale, regardless of the sticker price.

### Question 12

A contractual adjustment is like a store agreeing to accept a lower price and simply not charging the difference.

### Question 13

It is like a store honoring a coupon: the discount is the store's to absorb, and the customer is never asked to pay it back.

### Question 14

CO is like a 'the store will eat this cost' label on a receipt, while PR is 'the customer pays this.'

### Question 15

PR is like a 'customer pays this part' tag on the bill, telling the store exactly what to charge.

### Question 16

OA is like a 'miscellaneous' bucket on a receipt that the store manager decides how to handle.

### Question 17

Patient responsibility is like the share of a restaurant bill a friend's coupon does not cover, in three forms: a set entry fee, a portion of the year, and a percentage.

### Question 18

If the sticker price is $200 and the agreed price is $150, the store writes off the $50 difference.

### Question 19

If the agreed price is $150 and the plan pays $120, the patient's leftover share is the $30 difference.

### Question 20

The deductible is like a yearly 'pay the first $X yourself' amount; this claim just filled part of that bucket.

### Question 21

Coinsurance is like splitting a pizza 80/20: the plan pays for 80 slices out of 100 and you pay for 20.

### Question 22

If an item is not on the 'covered' list, it is like buying something a gift card does not cover, so the customer pays.

### Question 23

A denial is like a returned package; you open it, find the reason, and fix and resend it rather than throwing it away.

### Question 24

A CARC is like the short reason code on a store return receipt explaining why you got back less than you paid.

### Question 25

If the reason code is a short label, the RARC is the longer sentence underneath that explains it.

### Question 26

It is like a store agreeing to a sale price and then secretly charging the customer the original sticker price later.

### Question 27

PR is the only label that means 'ask the customer for this'; CO and OA go back to the store's own records.

### Question 28

The allowed amount is like the pre-agreed price in a contract between the store and the discount program.

### Question 29

It is like a price being capped by a coupon, so the store writes off the part above the cap.

### Question 30

The deductible is the part of the yearly 'pay yourself first' amount that lands on the patient's tab.

### Question 31

COB is like two gift cards covering one purchase; the store needs the first card's receipt before the second card can help.

### Question 32

Timely filing is like a 'return within 30 days' rule; send it in late and the store will not accept it.

### Question 33

Prior authorization is like needing a permission slip from the plan before the visit, and the claim says the slip was missing.

### Question 34

It is like a plan saying the service was not needed based on the notes, so it will not help pay.

### Question 35

A duplicate claim is like mailing the same letter twice; the second one is simply set aside.

### Question 36

PI is like a note from the plan saying 'we reduced this for our own reasons,' which the office then reviews.

### Question 37

A withhold is like a landlord holding a security deposit that may be returned later if everything checks out.

### Question 38

The billed amount is like a sticker price, and the payer pays the discounted agreed price instead.

### Question 39

It is like a cashier being handed $500 when the bill was $300; the honest move is to give back the extra $200.

### Question 40

A credit balance is like getting too much change back and needing to return the extra.

### Question 41

The copay is like a cover charge, but the deductible and coinsurance are extra portions of the bill that can still apply.

### Question 42

A write-off is like forgiving part of a bill; a refund is like handing back cash you already collected.

### Question 43

It is like making sure you put a deposit into the right person's bank account before typing in any numbers.

### Question 44

It is like a grocery receipt where some items are covered and some are not; you record each item exactly.

### Question 45

It is like counting the cash in the envelope against the amount written on it before entering it in the ledger.

### Question 46

Auto-posting is like a self-checkout machine; it is fast, but a person still checks that nothing scanned twice.

### Question 47

Reconciliation is like checking that the money in the register matches what the receipts say at closing time.

### Question 48

Posting the write-off is like marking a coupon discount on the exact line it applies to.

### Question 49

The leftover patient share stays on the patient's tab, like the part of a restaurant bill after a friend chips in.

### Question 50

An unapplied payment is like a deposit with no label yet, sitting in a 'to be sorted' tray.

### Question 51

Correcting an error is like fixing a wrong number in a ledger and noting who fixed it and when.

### Question 52

You never change what the receipt says just to make the math look neat; you record it exactly.

### Question 53

A denial is a 'needs attention' flag, not a dead end; someone must fix the reason and try again or decide the charge.

### Question 54

It is like checking a checklist so you do not deposit the same check into the register twice.

### Question 55

If the receipt and the cash do not match, you stop and ask a manager instead of guessing.

### Question 56

It is like marking a pre-paid ticket as already paid so no one asks for the money twice.

### Question 57

Before answering, you check the store's own records to see what is actually owed, then explain clearly.

### Question 58

A refund is like returning change you were overpaid; someone in charge checks the math before the money goes back.

### Question 59

Posting to the wrong payer is like depositing money into the wrong bank account; the records stop matching reality.

### Question 60

The secondary plan is like a second gift card that only works after the first card's receipt is attached.

### Question 61

Balancing is like making sure the cash register total equals the money in the drawer at the end of the day.

### Question 62

Collecting is taking the money; posting is writing it down in the ledger so the account is up to date.

### Question 63

If a service is not covered, the amount is moved to the patient's own tab rather than erased.

### Question 64

It is like a store deciding, by a set rule, not to chase a few cents, rather than making it up each time.

### Question 65

It is like a store offering a set payment plan instead of either demanding everything now or giving it away.

### Question 66

It is like finding money in an account with no deposit slip; you investigate where it really came from.

### Question 67

Accurate posting is like keeping a clean ledger so you always know exactly which bills are still unpaid.

### Question 68

It is like a stray deposit that must be matched to the right bill or returned to the sender.

### Question 69

A remittance is like one delivery with many labeled packages; each package goes to its own mailbox.

### Question 70

The statement is like a final tally that shows only what the patient genuinely still owes.

### Question 71

It is the 'your part' line on the receipt after the plan's portion is subtracted.

### Question 72

It is like a refund being sent to the customer instead of the store; the store checks with the customer before charging again.

### Question 73

It is like marking off a savings goal so everyone knows how much more must be paid before the plan starts helping.

### Question 74

For an out-of-network service, the plan uses its own price guide rather than the provider's sticker price.

### Question 75

The PLB segment is like a summary line at the bottom of a statement covering adjustments that apply to the whole account.

### Question 76

It is like an adjustment on the store's own summary account, not on any single customer's bill.

### Question 77

A recoupment is like a store taking back part of an earlier refund that was too large.

### Question 78

Take the $80 off the sticker price to reach $320, then the patient's 20% share of $320 is $64.

### Question 79

The secondary plan is like a second friend who chips in only on what is left after the first friend pays.

### Question 80

An audit trail is like a signed, dated note showing exactly who made each entry and when.

### Question 81

If two receipts disagree, you compare them to the original order and ask the company which is right before charging anyone.

### Question 82

Bundling is like a combo meal where the side item is already included and not charged separately.

### Question 83

Interest is like a small 'sorry for the wait' payment from the plan to the practice.

### Question 84

Waiving cost sharing without permission is like a cashier quietly not charging the required amount; it breaks the rules.

### Question 85

It is like processing a mixed stack of mail: each item gets handled by the right rule, and anything unusual goes to a manager.
